49.5 When making a conditional confirmation decision under section 13BA of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, the confirming authority will still need to consider whether there is a compelling case in the public interest for the making of the compulsory purchase order (including whether the acquiring authority has undertaken the steps outlined in paragraph 2.2).

49.6 A compulsory purchase order may be conditionally confirmed where the confirming authority considers the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the order has been established but there remains an outstanding impediment to the delivery of the underlying scheme which could be overcome by imposing a pre-exercise condition(s).

49.7 Pre-exercise condition(s) may not be imposed by the confirming authority to allow the compelling case in the public interest to be established by the acquiring authority at a later date.

49.8 The confirming authority may still consider it appropriate to confirm a compulsory purchase order without a pre-exercise condition(s) where there is an outstanding impediment.

50. What enabling compulsory purchase powers can the power to conditionally confirm compulsory purchase orders be used with?

50.1 Although the guidance on use of the power to confirm a compulsory purchase order subject to a pre-exercise condition(s) is predominately applicable to compulsory purchase orders made under the enabling powers listed in the Tier 2 section of this guidance, the power may be used by any enabling compulsory purchase power which is authorised under the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

50.2 The guidance on use of the power to confirm a compulsory purchase order subject to a pre-exercise condition(s) should be applied in accordance with other government departments’ guidance on the preparation, drafting and submission of compulsory purchase orders made under enabling powers which are not listed in the Tier 2 section of this guidance, for example, the Highways Act 1980.

51. When the confirming authority is considering using the power to conditionally confirm a compulsory purchase order, will the acquiring authority and objectors be given an opportunity to make representations?

51.1 Where the confirming authority is considering imposing pre-exercise condition(s), the confirming authority should notify, and give parties to the relevant compulsory purchase order, an opportunity to make representations including on the need for the imposition of a pre-exercise condition(s) and the proposed condition(s) wording.

51.2 Where objections to a compulsory purchase order are being considered by way of a public inquiry, the possible imposition of pre-exercise condition(s) may be discussed with the parties to the order via a roundtable topic session at the inquiry, for example, akin to a condition session in a planning appeal inquiry. Alternatively, where objections to a compulsory purchase order are being considered by way of exchange of written representations, the confirming authority may seek further representations from either party to the order on the possible imposition of pre-exercise condition(s).

52. What type of pre-exercise condition(s) may be imposed by the confirming authority when a compulsory purchase order is conditionally confirmed?

52.1 The circumstances and impediments to schemes being facilitated by use of compulsory purchase powers will differ from scheme-to-scheme and different considerations will affect the type of pre-exercise condition(s) which may be imposed.

52.2 The power to confirm a compulsory purchase order subject to pre-exercise conditions should be used sparingly and only when the confirming authority considers it necessary. It is not expected the power will be used where there are no impediments to the delivery of the underlying scheme or where the imposition of pre-exercise condition(s) will not be required to overcome an outstanding impediment.

52.3 It is expected only pre-exercise condition(s) which are genuinely capable of being complied with by the acquiring authority will be imposed when a compulsory purchase order is conditionally confirmed. It will be the confirming authority’s discretion as to what, and how many, pre-exercise conditions may be imposed when it conditionally confirms a compulsory purchase order. Pre-exercise conditions should not relate to matters which would usually be dealt with through the planning regime i.e. conditions attached to planning consents.

52.4 The government anticipates the power to conditionally confirm a compulsory purchase order will be used by confirming authorities in narrow circumstances.

52.5 In general, the following are examples which are provided for illustrative purposes of impediments in which the confirming authority may find it beneficial to impose a pre-exercise condition(s) through the conditional confirmation of a compulsory purchase order:

a landowner has refused to give a legal undertaking, for example, entered into a contract or development agreement with the acquiring authority, on when they will bring forward their alternative scheme on the land which they put forward at the public inquiry - the confirming authority could impose a condition that if the landowner doesn’t take action within a certain timescale, for example, bring forward a planning application or an application to discharge conditions on a planning permission, implement a planning permission, or build out a planning permission, the acquiring authority can make an application for the discharge of the pre-exercise condition

the funding to implement the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order (including the acquisition of the land) will not be released by the funder until the acquiring authority can provide a guarantee that it has ownership of the land - the confirming authority could impose a condition that the acquiring authority should, within a certain timescale, provide confirmation from the funder that it is willing to release the funding in light of the compelling case in the public interest being established (subject to confirmation the funding being made available) for use of a compulsory purchase order by the acquiring authority to acquire the land

a decision on the planning application, other consent (for example, Secretary of State consent for the disposal of land owned by a local council designated for its Housing Revenue Account) or licence needed to implement the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order is outstanding which will support the acquiring authority’s case the underlying scheme is deliverable - the confirming authority could impose a condition that the acquiring authority should, within a certain timescale, provide confirmation the planning permission, other consent or licence relating to the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order has been granted

52.6 The above illustrative examples do not indicate that the existence of those relevant circumstances must lead to the conditional confirmation of a compulsory purchase order. The confirming authority may still consider it appropriate to confirm a compulsory purchase order without a pre-exercise condition in those circumstances.

52.7 A pre-exercise condition(s) when drafted by the confirming authority and included in their conditional confirmation decision letter and/or decision report should be clear, concise and worded objectively. For example:

“The condition is that the development comprised in planning permission reference [insert reference number] has not been completed in accordance with that permission within 12 months of the date of this letter/report”

“The condition is that a development delivery agreement has been entered into by the interest holder of the land identified in column W, row X, Table Y in Schedule Z to the compulsory purchase order and the milestones set out in that agreement have not been met within 12 months of the date of this letter/report”

“The condition is the funding indicated by the acquiring authority, which is the subject of an outstanding application at the time of this decision, is in place (whether or not due to the success of the application) within 3 months of the date of this letter/report”

53. What type of pre-exercise condition(s) should not be imposed?

53.1 A pre-exercise condition(s) will not be required where the compelling case in the public interest for the making of a compulsory purchase order can be established without the need for a pre-exercise condition(s) being met.

53.2 Use of a compulsory purchase power concerns only the compulsory acquisition of land. A pre-exercise condition(s) relating to, for example, the design, construction practices or other such matters associated with the underlying scheme should not be imposed.

53.3 Similarly, a pre-exercise condition(s) relating to matters associated with the assessment and determination of compensation should not be imposed.

54. What is the effect of the conditional confirmation of a compulsory purchase order?

54.1 Where a compulsory purchase order is conditionally confirmed, the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the compulsory purchase order will be established subject to the relevant condition(s) being met. The relevant order and associated compulsory purchase power will not become operative or in force until the confirming authority has decided, on an application made by the acquiring authority, that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met. Where there is more than one pre-exercise condition, all the conditions will have to be met before the relevant compulsory purchase order and associated compulsory purchase power can become operative.

54.2 When making its decision on an application by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, the confirming authority will not re-consider the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the compulsory purchase order. 54.3 The compulsory purchase order will expire and the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the order will fall away if:

(a) the confirming authority has not received an application from the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, which must be made by the deadline specified by the confirming authority when it conditionally confirmed the compulsory purchase order, or

(b) having received such an application by that deadline, the confirming authority decides the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have not been met.

55. How many applications may the acquiring authority make to the confirming authority that pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met?

55.1 To avoid causing uncertainty and anxiety for those with an interest in the land subject of the conditionally confirmed compulsory purchase order, particularly where the order is subject to more than one condition, acquiring authorities should only make one application to the confirming authority when they consider the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met.

55.2 Where an application has been submitted by the acquiring authority and the confirming authority decides the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have not been met, the compulsory purchase order will expire and there will be no order for which the authority can submit a new application.

56. How will the parties to a compulsory purchase order be notified of a decision by the confirming authority to conditionally confirm the order including the associated pre-exercise condition(s)?

56.1 The confirming authority, when issuing its decision to conditionally confirm a compulsory purchase order, will include in its decision letter the pre-exercise condition(s) it has imposed and state the deadline for when an application is to be made by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met. The decision letter should also outline the reasoning for imposing the condition(s).

56.2 When setting the deadline for the submission of an application by the acquiring authority, the confirming authority should ensure a proportionate balance is struck between providing a reasonable time-period for compliance by the relevant acquiring authority and reducing prolonged periods of uncertainty for those with an interest in the land subject of the conditionally confirmed compulsory purchase order.

56.3 The associated confirmation notice required to be served and affixed to land by the acquiring authority under section 15 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 (using Form 10 in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 9] will state the:

(a) pre-exercise condition(s) imposed by the confirming authority,

(b) deadline specified by the confirming authority for when an application is to be made by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, and

(c) that the relevant compulsory purchase order will not become operative until the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met

56.4 Where 1. a compulsory purchase order has been conditionally confirmed, there is no requirement for acquiring authorities to publish a confirmation notice in a newspaper or on a website which contains information about the scheme or project that underlies the proposed purchase (section 15(3) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981)[footnote 10]. The following requirements on acquiring authorities under section 15(1) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 remain unchanged:

serve a confirmation notice on each person on whom a notice was required to be served under section 12 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, and

affix a confirmation notice on or near the land included in the compulsory purchase order

57. Will objectors be able to comment on an application by the acquiring authority that a pre-exercise condition(s) has been met?

57.1 Only relevant objectors to a compulsory purchase order which has been conditionally confirmed will be given notice of an application by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) in its opinion has/have been met and have the opportunity to make written representations in response to the application[footnote 11].

57.2 Any representations made by a relevant objector relating to the confirming authority’s previous decision to conditionally confirm the compulsory purchase order, i.e. whether or not the compulsory purchase order should have been conditionally confirmed in the first place (including the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the compulsory purchase order), or matters related to compensation, will not be considered. Representations will be considered to the extent they are material to the question of whether the relevant pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met.

57.3 The procedure to be followed in relation to the making of an application by the acquiring authority that a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, including how relevant objectors are to be given notice of an application together with the opportunity to make representations, is outlined in the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Conditional Confirmation) Regulations 2026.

57.4 When making a decision on an application made by the acquiring authority that a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, the confirming authority will not re-consider the compelling case in the public interest for the making of the compulsory purchase order. The confirming authority’s decision on an application by the acquiring authority will focus only on whether or not the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met.

58. How long could a pre-exercise condition be imposed for?

58.1 The deadline for the making of an application by the acquiring authority that a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met will depend on the circumstances of the individual compulsory purchase order and the timescale in which it was decided by the confirming authority that the relevant issue, subject of the condition, should be resolved by. It will be the confirming authority’s discretion to determine the appropriate timescale for when an application that a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met should be submitted. When determining the appropriate timescale, the confirming authority should ensure prolonged periods of uncertainty for landowners and relevant objectors are avoided wherever possible.

59. How will relevant objectors be notified of the confirming authority’s decision on whether a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met?

59.1 Where a compulsory purchase order was conditionally confirmed, and the confirming authority decides on an application made by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, the acquiring authority must within six weeks of the confirming authority’s decision or any longer period as agreed between the acquiring authority and confirming authority:

(a) serve a copy of the order and a fulfilment notice on each person on whom a notice was required to be served under section 12 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 Act,

(b) affix a fulfilment notice to the land comprised in the order, and

(c) publish a fulfilment notice in a newspaper

59.2 The acquiring authority must also publish a fulfilment notice on a website which contains information about the scheme or project that underlies the proposed purchase until the end of the period of six weeks, beginning with the day on which the acquiring authority serves the copy of the order and a fulfilment notice on relevant persons (see (a) above).

59.3 The fulfilment notice will:

state that the condition(s) subject to which the compulsory purchase order was confirmed has/have been met and that the compulsory purchase order will therefore become operative, and

annex the information contained the confirmation notice which was served when the compulsory purchase order was conditionally confirmed

Forms 11B and 11C in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 12] prescribe the form which the fulfilment notice should take.

59.4 Where a compulsory purchase order was conditionally confirmed and the confirming authority makes a decision on an application made by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, regardless of the decision, the acquiring authority and each relevant objectors to the relevant order will be notified in writing of the confirming authority’s decision along with its reasons for reaching that decision.

60. Where a confirming authority decides a pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, when can the relevant compulsory purchase power be exercised?

60.1 Where a compulsory purchase order was conditionally confirmed, and the confirming authority decides on an application made by the acquiring authority that the pre-exercise condition(s) has/have been met, the order will become operative and in force on the date on which a fulfilment notice in respect of the order is first published as required by section 15(4C)(b)(i) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

61. When can a compulsory purchase order be confirmed by the acquiring authority?

61.1 Section 14A of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 provides a discretionary power for the confirming authority to give the acquiring authority notice that it may decide an order which has been submitted for confirmation if certain specified conditions are met.

61.2 When deciding whether to give notice to the acquiring authority under section 14A(1) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, the confirming authority must be satisfied that:

there are no outstanding objections to the order

all the statutory requirements as to the service and publication of notices have been complied with

the order is capable of being confirmed without modification or with such modification that it has specified

The power of the confirming authority to give a notice under section 14A(1) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 is excluded in cases where:

the land to be acquired includes land acquired by a statutory undertaker for the purposes of its undertaking, that statutory undertaker has made representations to the minister responsible for sponsoring its business and the confirming authority is satisfied that the land to be taken is used for the purposes of the undertaking

the land to be acquired forms part of a common, open space, or fuel or field garden allotment

as confirmation of an order in these circumstances is contingent on other ministerial decisions.

61.3 The power for the confirming authority to issue a notice for the acquiring authority to confirm its own compulsory purchase order applies where the acquiring authority has made a compulsory purchase order which includes a direction applying section 14A of the Land Compensation Act 1961 (see Can an acquiring authority confirm its own compulsory purchase order if it includes a direction applying section 14A of the Land Compensation Act 1961?).

61.4 The acquiring authority’s power to confirm a compulsory purchase order does not extend to confirming the order in stages.

62. What should the confirming authority do if it decides to give an acquiring authority the power to confirm a compulsory purchase order?

62.1 To exercise its discretionary power under section 14A of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, the confirming authority will serve a notice on the acquiring authority giving it the power to confirm the compulsory purchase order (section 14A(1) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981). The sealed order and one sealed map (or sets of sealed maps) will be returned with the notice. The notice should:

indicate that if the acquiring authority decides to confirm the order, it should be endorsed as confirmed with the endorsement authenticated by a person having authority to do so

suggest a form of words for the endorsement

refer to the statutory requirement to serve notice of confirmation under section 15 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981

require that the confirming authority should be informed of the decision on the order as soon as possible with (where applicable) a copy of the endorsed order

where appropriate, specify the modifications which the acquiring authority may make to the order

63. How will the confirming authority decide whether modifications are required to a compulsory purchase order which are to be made by the acquiring authority?

63.1 When considering whether it is appropriate to exercise the power under section 14A of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 to allow the acquiring authority to confirm its own compulsory purchase order, the confirming authority will undertake the procedural checks of the compulsory purchase order listed under paragraph 61.2 of this guidance and then consider whether any modifications are required to the order to ensure its legal accuracy, and if so, what those modifications are.

64. What modifications to a compulsory purchase order is an acquiring authority able to make when confirming it?

64.1 When confirming its own compulsory purchase order under section 14A of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, the acquiring authority may only make a modification specified by the confirming authority. The confirming authority may only specify a modification to the order which would:

(a) add an additional interest in the land (the confirming authority must be satisfied that the interest holder consents to the proposed modification),

(b) remove an interest in any land to which the order applies,

(c) remove part of an interest in any land to which the order applies (the confirming authority must be satisfied that the interest holder consents to the proposed modification), or

(d) not affect any interests in the land.

Neither the confirming authority nor the acquiring authority will be allowed to modify the order to include additional land without the consent of the landowner (section 14 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981).

64.2 Examples of the types of modifications which the acquiring authority may make to a compulsory purchase order when confirming it may include (and are not limited to):

rectifying discrepancies between the order text (including schedule) and map such as modifying the colour used to identify plots of land on the map to reflect the wording used in the order text

removing an interest or plot of land from an order schedule and/or map (often done with ink to strike through an interest in one of the tables in the schedule and/or the red line boundary on the map) where the acquiring authority no longer proposes to acquire that land through the compulsory purchase process

inserting a new interest in the order schedule and map where the person has agreed for their interest to be included

correcting grammatical or spelling errors in the order text, schedule or map

inserting dashes (-) or “n/a” into all the blank entries in Tables 1 and 2 of an order schedule

amending the title of the map to match the title of the order

inserting definitions of the relevant Acts (e.g. “The Town and Country Planning Act 1990”; “The Acquisition of Land Act 1981”) in the order text

65. What should the acquiring authority do if it decides to confirm its own order?

65.1 If the acquiring authority decides to confirm its own order, it should return the notice of confirmation to the confirming authority. The form of the notice of confirmation is set out in Form 11 in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 13].

65.2 An acquiring authority exercising the power to confirm must notify the confirming authority as soon as reasonably practicable of its decision (section 14A(6) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981). Until such notification is received, the confirming authority can revoke the acquiring authority’s power to confirm. This might be necessary, for example, if the confirming authority received a late objection which raised important issues or if the acquiring authority failed to decide whether to confirm the compulsory purchase order within a reasonable timescale.

Acquiring authorities are asked to ensure that in all cases the confirming department is notified without delay of the date when notice of confirmation of the order is first published in the newspaper in accordance with the provisions of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

65.3 This is important as the 6 weeks’ period allowed by virtue of section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 for an application to the High Court to be made begins on this date. Similarly, and for the same reason, where the Secretary of State has given a certificate under section 19 of, or paragraph 6 of Schedule 3 to, the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, the department giving the certificate should be notified straight away of the date when notice is first published.

The form of the notice of confirmation by an acquiring authority in a newspaper is set out in Form 11A in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 14].

65.4 Where the acquiring authority has determined to confirm its own compulsory purchase order with modifications, it must, at the same time as notifying the confirming authority of its decision:

(a) provide the confirming authority with a copy of the order as modified, and

(b) certify that the only modifications it made to the order were those specified by the confirming authority when it gave its notice under section 14A(1) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

66. Are there timetables for confirmation of compulsory purchase orders?

66.1 Section 14B of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981[footnote 15] requires the Secretary of State to publish one or more timetables for confirmation of compulsory purchase orders. The timescales are set out in the paragraphs which follow. The target timescales will apply to all confirming authorities other than the Welsh Ministers (who have the power to publish their own timetables under section 14C of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 in relation to compulsory purchase orders to be confirmed by them).

67. How long will it take to get a decision on a compulsory purchase order which is delegated to an inspector and subject to the written representations procedure?

67.1 Where a compulsory purchase order is delegated to an inspector and subject to the written representation procedure, there is a statutory requirement for a site visit, where necessary, to be conducted within 15 weeks of the starting date letter (see regulation 8(1) of the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Written Representations Procedure) (Ministers) Regulations 2004[footnote 16]).

67.2 A decision should be issued within 4 weeks of the site visit date in 80% of cases delegated by the Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority; with 100% of cases being decided within 8 weeks of the site visit date.

67.3 In cases where there has not been a site visit, the timescales for decision will be taken from the final exchange of representations under regulation 5 of the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Written Representations Procedure) (Ministers) Regulations 2004.

68. How long will it take to get a decision on a compulsory purchase order which is delegated to an inspector and subject to the public inquiry procedure?

68.1 Where a compulsory purchase order is delegated to an inspector and subject to the public inquiry procedure under the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Inquiries Procedure) Rules 2007, within 10 working days beginning with the day after the inquiry closes, the parties will be notified of the expected date on which a decision will be issued (see rule 18 in Schedule 1 to the Compulsory Purchase (Inquiries Procedure) Rules 2007[footnote 17]).

68.2 A decision on the compulsory purchase order should be issued by the inspector within 8 weeks of the close of the inquiry in 80% of cases delegated by the Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority; with 100% of cases being decided within 12 weeks.

69. How long will it take to get a decision on a compulsory purchase order which is decided by a Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority and subject to the written representations procedure?

69.1 Where a compulsory purchase order is subject to the written representations procedure, there is a statutory requirement for a site visit, where necessary, to be conducted within 15 weeks of the starting date letter (see regulation 8(1) of the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Written Representations Procedure) (Ministers) Regulations 2004[footnote 18]).

69.2 The Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority should issue 80% of compulsory purchase decisions on written representation cases within 8 weeks of the site visit. The remaining 20% of cases should be decided within 12 weeks of the site visit.

69.3 In cases where there has not been a site visit, the timescales for decision will be taken from the final exchange of representations under regulation 5 of the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Written Representations Procedure) (Ministers) Regulations 2004.

70. How long will it take to get a decision on a compulsory purchase order which is decided by a Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority and subject to the public inquiry procedure?

70.1 Where a compulsory purchase order is to be decided by the Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority and subject to the public inquiry procedure, the parties will be notified within 10 working days beginning with the day after the inquiry closes of the expected date of the Secretary of State’s decision (see rule 18(A1) of the Compulsory Purchase (Inquiries Procedure) Rules 2007[footnote 19]).

70.2 In addition, there is a target that 80% of cases should be decided by the relevant Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority within 20 weeks of the close of the public inquiry – with the remaining cases decided within 24 weeks.

71. What happens if the Secretary of State in their role as the confirming authority or an inspector fails to issue a decision in accordance with the published timescales?

71.1 The Secretary of State who has responsibility for housing and planning matters must issue an annual report to Parliament showing the extent to which confirming authorities have complied with the published timescales.

71.2 The validity of a compulsory purchase order is not, however, affected by any failure to comply with a timetable (see section 14B(4) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981).

72. Can a compulsory purchase order be challenged through the courts after it has been confirmed?

72.1 Any 1. person aggrieved who wishes to dispute the validity of a compulsory purchase order, or any of its provisions, can challenge the order through an application to the High Court under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 on the grounds that:

the authorisation of the order is not empowered to be granted under the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 or an enactment mentioned in section 1(1) of that Act

a ‘relevant requirement’ has not been complied with

72.2 A ‘relevant requirement’ is any requirement under the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, of any regulations made under it, or the Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992 or of regulations made under that act.

72.3 Any such application must be made within 6 weeks of the date specified in section 23(4) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

73. What powers does the court have on an application under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981?

73.1 Section 24 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 sets out the powers of the court on an application under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981. First, the court has the discretionary power to grant interim relief suspending the operation of the order or certificate pending the final determination of the court proceedings (section 24(1)). Second, where a challenge under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 is successful, the court has the discretionary power to quash:

the decision to confirm the compulsory purchase order (section 24(3)) (NB: this does not apply in relation to an application under section 23 which was made before 13 July 2016)

the whole or any part of an order (section 24(2))

74. Is the time period for implementing a compulsory purchase order extended where it is the subject of a legal challenge?

74.1 Under section 4A of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965 (for notice to treat process) and section 5B of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 (for general vesting declaration process) the applicable period for implementing a compulsory purchase order is extended for:

a period equivalent to the period from the date an application challenging the order is made until it is withdrawn or finally determined

one year

whichever is the shorter. NB: The extended time period does not apply to an application made in respect of a compulsory purchase order which became operative before 13 July 2016.

74.2 An application to challenge an order is finally determined after the normal time for submitting an appeal has elapsed or, where an appeal has been submitted, it is either withdrawn or finally determined.

75. Can a decision not to confirm a compulsory purchase order be challenged through the courts?

75.1 A decision not to confirm a compulsory purchase order can be challenged through the courts by means of an application for judicial review under Part 54 of the Civil Procedure Rules 1998.

76. Is there a record of compulsory purchase orders decisions?

76.1 A public register of compulsory purchase order decisions for cases which the Secretary of State who has responsibility for housing and planning matters is the confirming authority for (along with decisions issued by inspectors on behalf of the Secretary of State) is maintained on our website.

77. What happens if the acquiring authority wishes to withdraw its compulsory purchase order?

77.1 An unconfirmed compulsory purchase order will result in the compulsory purchase of the land not being authorised. Acquiring authorities should consider the reasons for non-confirmation and decide whether or not they wish to pursue a new compulsory purchase order or seek alternative resolutions to acquire the land within the framework and principles of published guidance on the acquisition of assets. Following the making of a compulsory purchase order, there may be instances where the acquiring authority may wish to withdraw the order and make a resolution not to seek its confirmation. For example, where an underlying scheme is no longer proceeding, a blight notice has been served on the acquiring authority or an agreement has been reached with landowners. In these circumstances, the acquiring authority may submit a request to the confirming authority asking it not confirm the compulsory purchase order. Such requests should be accompanied by evidence of the acquiring authority’s decision to withdraw its compulsory purchase order. Where a request is accepted by the confirming authority, it will note in the response that the acquiring authority has decided to withdraw its compulsory purchase order and that the acquiring authority should inform all appropriate persons to the order of the acquiring authority’s decision.

Stage 5: Implementing a compulsory purchase order

78. When does a compulsory purchase order become operative?

78.1 Unless the acquisition is subject to the special parliamentary procedure (for example, in the case of certain special kinds of land), a compulsory purchase order which has been confirmed becomes operative on the date on which the notice of its confirmation (‘confirmation notice’) is first published.

78.2 The method of publication and the information which must be included in a confirmation notice is set out in section 15 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 and includes:

publishing a copy of the notice on a website and in a newspaper (except where a compulsory purchase order is conditionally confirmed – see How will the parties to a compulsory purchase order be notified of a decision by the confirming authority to conditionally confirm the order including the associated pre-exercise condition(s)?) in the locality in which the land comprised in the order is situated (see What format should a newspaper notice of the confirmation of a compulsory purchase order adopt?)

affixing a copy of the notice on or near the land included in the compulsory purchase order

serving a copy of the notice along with a copy of the confirmed compulsory purchase order on each person on whom a notice was required to be served under section 12 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981.

Confirmation notices must also:

contain a prescribed statement about the effect of Parts 2 and 3 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 set out in in Form 9A in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 20]

invite any person who would be entitled to claim compensation if a declaration were executed under section 4 of that Act to give the acquiring authority information about the person’s name, address and interest in land, using a prescribed form which is set out in Form 10 (where confirmation of the compulsory purchase order is not undertaken by the acquiring authority) or Form 11 (where confirmation of the compulsory purchase order is undertaken by the acquiring authority) in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 21]

78.3 Where a compulsory purchase order which includes a direction applying section 14A of the Land Compensation Act 1961 is confirmed, additional information must be included in the confirmation notice (see How will landowners be notified of a compulsory purchase order which has been confirmed with a direction applying section 14A of the Land Compensation Act 1961 included?).

78.4 Acquiring authorities must issue the confirmation notice within 6 weeks of the date of the order being confirmed or such longer period as may be agreed between the acquiring authority and the confirming authority (section 15(3A) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981). Where an acquiring authority fails to do so, the confirming authority may take the necessary steps itself and recover its reasonable costs of doing so from the acquiring authority.

79. What format should a newspaper notice of the confirmation of a compulsory purchase order adopt?

79.1 The notice of the confirmation of the compulsory purchase order required to be published in a newspaper should comply with Form 10A or Form 11A (where the order is confirmed by the acquiring authority) in the Schedule to the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Prescribed Forms) (Ministers) Regulations 2004 (as amended)[footnote 22].

79.2 When describing the land in the newspaper notice, instead of describing the land using the wording included in the schedule to the compulsory purchase order, the notice may briefly identify the land by giving its postal address, if available, or otherwise. For example, instead of identifying the relevant land as:

“4826 square metres part of the pastureland including bed of stream, culverted watercourses and associated headwalls of Strawberry Fields Farm on the south-west of A4999 Ellie Roundabout, on the north-west of Strawberry Fields Farm residential buildings” the acquiring authority could identify it as “part of the pastureland including bed of stream, culverted watercourses and associated headwalls of Strawberry Fields Farm”

“all interests in 81.7 square metres of vacant dwelling house 5 Liverpool Terrace, Blackburn, B83 4DD” the acquiring authority could identify the relevant land as “5 Liverpool Terrace, Blackburn, B83 4DD”

“The dwellinghouse situated at Burnley Lancashire together with the appurtenances thereto known as 10a and 10b Heathcliffe Road Burnley BB99 1OE and 40 Rover Street Burnley BB98 1QE” the acquiring authority could identify the relevant land as “10a and 10b Heathcliffe Road Burnley BB99 1OE and 40 Rover Street Burnley BB98 1QE”

80. How do I register a confirmation notice as a local land charge?

80.1 Section 15(6) of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 provides that a confirmation notice should be sent by the acquiring authority to the Chief Land Registrar and that it shall be a local land charge. Where land in the order is situated in an area for which the local authority remains the registering authority for local land charges (i.e. where the changes made by Parts 1 and 3 of Schedule 5 to the Infrastructure Act 2015 have not yet taken effect in that local authority area), the acquiring authority should comply with the steps required by section 5 of the Local Land Charges Act 1975 (prior to it being amended by the Infrastructure Act 2015) to ensure that the charge is registered.

81. How can Charity Trustees convey land to a public authority?

81.1 If acquiring land from a charity, acquiring authorities should be aware of the provisions in Part 7 of the Charities Act 2011 and may need to consult the Charity Commission.

82. How do acquiring authorities take possession of land following the confirmation of a compulsory purchase order?

82.1 Following confirmation of a compulsory purchase order, except where it has been confirmed subject to pre-exercise conditions, the acquiring authority may then exercise the compulsory purchase power (unless the operation of the compulsory purchase order is suspended by the High Court). The actual acquisition process will proceed by one of two routes - either by the acquiring authority serving a notice to treat or by executing a general vesting declaration.

83. What is a notice to treat?

83.1 There is no prescribed form for a notice to treat but the document must:

describe the land to which it relates

demand particulars of the interest in the land

demand particulars of the compensation claim of the recipient

state that the acquiring authority is willing to treat for the purchase of the land and for compensation for any damage caused by the execution of the works

83.2 Possession cannot normally be taken until the acquiring authority has served a notice of entry and the minimum period specified in that notice has expired.

83.3 Title to the land is subsequently transferred by a normal conveyance.

84. When should a notice to treat be served?

84.1 Under section 4 of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965, a notice to treat may not be served after the end of the period of three years beginning with the date on which the compulsory purchase order becomes operative. The confirming authority does however have the power under section 13D of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 to extend this time limit. This may prove useful where an acquiring authority wishes to bring forward a compulsory purchase order for the whole of a staged development and the later stages of the development may not have been planned for delivery until more than 3 years from when the order becomes operative. Likewise, an acquiring authority may make a compulsory purchase order earlier in the delivery of its scheme to ensure it has certainty over land assembly knowing there is the possibility of the conditional confirmation of the order. This may in turn mean that the period between the compulsory purchase order becoming operative and delivery of the scheme is longer than three years. Once served, the notice to treat then remains effective for a further 3 years under section 5(2A) of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965.

84.2 It can be very stressful for those directly affected to know that a compulsory purchase order has been confirmed on their land or property. The prospect of a period of up to 6 years (and possibly longer where the time limit is extended by the confirming authority under section 13D of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981) before the acquiring authority actually takes possession can be daunting. Acquiring authorities are therefore urged to keep such people fully informed using clear and easy to understand, non-technical language about the various processes involved and of their likely timing. In addition to keeping open the possibility of earlier acquisition where requested by an owner.

85. What period of notice should be given before taking possession under the notice to treat process?

85.1 Once the crucial stage of actually taking possession is reached, the acquiring authority is required by section 11 of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965 (“the 1965 Act”) to serve a notice of its intention to gain entry.

In respect of a compulsory purchase order which is confirmed on or after 3 February 2017, the notice period will be not less than 3 months beginning with the date of service of the notice, except in either of the following circumstances:

where it is a notice to which section 11A(4) of the 1965 Act applies (i.e. where it is being served on a ‘newly identified person’ under section 11A(1)(b) and that person is not an occupier, or the acquiring authority was unaware of the person because they received misleading information in response to their inquiries under section 5(1) of the 1965 Act) - in these circumstances, section 11A(4) provides for a shorter minimum notice period

where it is a notice to which paragraph 13 of Schedule 2A to the 1965 Act applies (i.e. where under the material detriment provisions in that schedule, an acquiring authority is permitted to serve a further notice of entry, after the initial notice of entry ceased to have effect under paragraph 6, in respect of the land proposed to be acquired)

85.2 Although it is necessary for a notice to treat to have been served, this can be done at the same time as serving the notice of entry. A notice of entry cannot be served after a notice to treat has ceased to be effective. A notice to treat can only be withdrawn in limited circumstances.

85.3 Acquiring authorities are encouraged to negotiate a mutually convenient date of entry with the claimant. It is good practice for the acquiring authority to:

give owners and occupiers (where appropriate) an indication of the approximate date when possession will be taken when serving the notice to treat

consider the steps which those being dispossessed will need to take to vacate their properties before deciding on the timing of actually taking possession

85.4 Authorities should also be aware that:

agricultural landowners or tenants may need to know the date for the notice of entry earlier than others because of crop cycles and the need to find alternative premises

short notice often results in higher compensation claims

until there is an actual or deemed notice to treat an occupier is at risk that any costs they incur in anticipation of receiving such a notice may not be claimable; acquiring authorities would be advised to analyse how long it will take most occupiers to relocate and if the notice of entry is inadequate then they should consider giving an earlier commitment to pay certain costs such as their reasonable costs in identifying suitable alternative accommodation

85.5 It is usually important to make an accurate record of the physical condition of the land at the valuation date.

86. What happens if the acquiring authority does not take possession at the time specified in the notice of entry?

86.1 Where a compulsory purchase of land has been authorised on or after 3 February 2017 (i.e. where the order was confirmed on or after that date), section 11B of the Compulsory Purchase Act 1965 allows occupiers with an interest in the land to serve a counter-notice on an acquiring authority to require entry on a specified date which must not be earlier than the date specified in the notice of entry. The occupier must give at least 28 days’ notice of the date they want entry to be taken.

87. What is a general vesting declaration?

87.1 A general vesting declaration can be used as an alternative to the notice to treat procedure. It replaces the notice to treat, notice of entry and the conveyance with one procedure which automatically vests title in the land with the acquiring authority on a certain date.

87.2 General vesting declarations are made under the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 and in accordance with the Compulsory Purchase of Land (Vesting Declarations) (England) Regulations 2017[footnote 23].

88. When might a general vesting declaration be used?

88.1 An acquiring authority may prefer to proceed by general vesting declaration as this enables the authority to obtain title to the land without having first to be satisfied as to the vendor’s title or to settle the amount of compensation (subject to any special procedures such as in relation to purchase of commoners’ rights: see section 21 of, and Schedule 4 to, Compulsory Purchase Act 1965). It can therefore be particularly useful where:

some of the owners are unknown

the authority wishes to obtain title with minimum delay (for example, to dispose of the land to developers)

88.2 A general vesting declaration may be made for any part or all of the land included in the compulsory purchase order except where an acquiring authority has already served (and not withdrawn) a notice to treat in respect of that land.

88.3 Section 4(1B) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 makes clear that the above exception does not apply to deemed notices to treat that may, for example, arise from a blight notice or purchase notice.

88.4 For minor tenancies and long tenancies which are about to expire, a general vesting declaration will also not be effective. However, there is a special procedure set out in section 9 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 for dealing with them.

88.5 Where unregistered land is acquired by general vesting declaration, acquiring authorities are recommended to voluntarily apply for first registration under section 3 of the Land Registration Act 2002.

89. When should a general vesting declaration be served?

89.1 For compulsory purchase orders which become operative on or after 13 July 2016, section 5A of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 makes clear that a general vesting declaration may not be executed after the end of the period of 3 years beginning with the day on which the compulsory purchase order becomes operative. The confirming authority does however have the power under section 13D of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 to extend this time limit. This may prove useful where an acquiring authority wishes to bring forward a compulsory purchase order for the whole of a staged development and the later stages of the development may not have been planned for delivery until more than 3 years from when the order becomes operative. Likewise, an acquiring authority may make a compulsory purchase order earlier in the delivery of its scheme to ensure it has certainty over land assembly knowing there is the possibility of the conditional confirmation of the order. This may in turn mean that the period between the compulsory purchase order becoming operative and delivery of the scheme is longer than 3 years.

90. How does the acquiring authority make a general vesting declaration if the owner, lessee or occupier is unknown?

90.1 If it is not possible (after reasonable inquiry) to ascertain the name or address of an owner, lessee or occupier of land, the acquiring authority should comply with section 329(2) of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 when serving the notice after executing the general declaration (required under section 6 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981).

91. What period of notice should be given before taking possession under the general vesting declaration process?

91.1 For a compulsory purchase of land authorised on or after 3 February 2017, the acquiring authority must usually give at least three months’ notice before taking possession under section 4(1) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981. Acquiring authorities should consider how long it will take occupiers to reasonably relocate and if three months is considered insufficient, consider increasing the vesting period (and therefore the notice period). Acquiring authorities and the owner of the relevant interest may postpone the vesting of the interest in the acquiring authority by written agreement and agree a different vesting date under section 8A of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981.

92. Are there any circumstances where acquiring authorities can take possession of land earlier?

92.1 In certain circumstances, acquiring authorities may give less than three months’ notice before taking possession of land. These are where the following conditions have been met (section 4A(1) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981[[footnote 24]:

(a) the land subject of the compulsory purchase is unoccupied (if the land is occupied only by a person who does not have a right to occupy it, then it is to be treated as if it is unoccupied),

(b) the acquiring authority considers that, by reason of disrepair, neglect, contamination, or risk to health or safety, the land subject of the compulsory purchase is unfit for its ‘ordinary use’[footnote 25], and

(c) a person with an interest in the land subject of the compulsory purchase is unable to serve a counter-notice under paragraph 2 of Schedule A1 to the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981.

92.2 Acquiring authorities may also give less than three months’ notice before taking possession of land where, after reasonable inquiry, they have been unable to identify any person with an interest in the land subject to the compulsory purchase order (section 4A(2) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981[footnote 26]).

92.3 Illustrative examples of circumstances where acquiring authorities may take possession of land earlier include:

Scenario 1: Land in a town centre which subsists three derelict, empty buildings that were previously occupied for particular uses and is subject to a compulsory purchase order made under section 226 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990. The particular uses were a shop providing office supplies; a jeweller; and an office for a local care provider. As the three buildings are in a state of disrepair, neglected and a risk to health and safety, none of them can be immediately occupied and their former uses resumed without works being undertaken to make the buildings safe and habitable.

Once the general vesting declaration is executed, instead of giving a minimum of three months’ notice before taking possession of the land, the local authority can take possession after giving six weeks’ notice.

Scenario 2: A local authority makes a compulsory purchase order under section 17 of the Housing Act 1985 to acquire a derelict house which has no occupiers. The local authority executes a general vesting declaration to enter and take possession of the property shortly after publishing the confirmation notice in accordance with section 15 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981. Once the general vesting declaration is executed, instead of giving a minimum of three months’ notice before taking possession of the property, the local authority can take possession after giving six weeks’ notice.

Scenario 3: A local authority makes a compulsory purchase order under section 226 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 to acquire land to facilitate a mixed-use town centre regeneration scheme. Following confirmation of the compulsory purchase order, despite the local authority serving, publishing and affixing confirmation notices in accordance with section 15 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981, in addition to making specific enquiries into the ownership of the land, the authority is unable to identify the landowner. Instead of giving a minimum of three months’ notice before taking possession of the land subject to the compulsory purchase order after executing a general vesting declaration, the local authority may take possession after six weeks’ notice.

92.4 The power for acquiring authorities to give less than three months’ notice before taking possession of land does not apply to compulsory acquisitions authorised before 18 February 2026 (i.e. the date section 108 of the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025 came into force).

92.5 It will be for acquiring authorities to identify where they think the circumstances allowing them to take early possession of land or property exist and to defend any disputes or challenges made on use of the power to take early possession of land under section 4A(1) and (2) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981.

92.6 Where 1. the acquiring authority considers the circumstances allowing them to give less than three months’ notice before taking possession of land have been met, and they execute a general vesting declaration in respect of any of the land which they are authorised to acquire by the compulsory purchase order, the land may vest in the authority from the end of a period of not less than six weeks from the date on which the service of notices required by section 6 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 is completed.

92.7 Regardless of the condition or occupation status of the land, acquiring authorities and the owner of a relevant interest in land may also by written agreement allow for their interest to vest in the acquiring authority before the end of the normal three months’ notice period (section 8B of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981[footnote 27]). The agreed date may not be before the last day on which a person may bring proceedings for disputing the validity of a compulsory purchase order, or any of its provisions, through an application to the High Court under section 23 of the Acquisition of Land Act 1981 i.e. six weeks from the date on which notice of the confirmation of the order is first published in accordance with the Acquisition of Land Act 1981. Where an owner of a relevant interest in land enters into an agreement with the acquiring authority under section 8B of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981, they will be unable to serve a counter-notice under paragraph 2 of Schedule A1 to the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981.

93. Can a person challenge an acquiring authority’s decision to take early possession of land without the agreement of the owner?

93.1 At any time before the end of the period of four weeks beginning with the date on which the acquiring authority executes a general vesting declaration to take early possession of land where there is no agreement with the relevant interest holder, a person may make representations to the authority that the circumstances allowing it to take early possession of land do not apply (section 4B of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981). Representations may be made verbally or in writing to the acquiring authority which must provide a written response no later than seven days after first receiving the representations (section 4B(2) and (4) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981).

93.2 If, before the land vests in the acquiring authority, the authority becomes aware that the circumstances allowing it to take early possession of land in fact do not apply, it must amend the general vesting declaration so that the land will not vest in the authority until a period of not less than three months from the date service of notices under section 6 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981 was completed (section 4B(5) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981). Where the acquiring authority amends a general vesting declaration, it must notify every person who:

(a) made a representation, and

(b) was served a notice about the general vesting declaration under section 6 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981.

94. What notification must the acquiring authority undertake when it intends to take early possession of land without the agreement of the owner?

94.1 Where the acquiring authority considers the conditions allowing them to give less than three months’ notice before taking possession of land have been met, when serving the notice under section 6 of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981[footnote 28], the notice will:

(a) make clear the acquiring authority considers the conditions allowing it to take early possession of land are available,

(b) state what the vesting date of the land is,

(c) explain that any person who disagrees with the acquiring authority’s view that it may take early possession of land can make representations to the acquiring authority, and

(d) confirm that if, before the vesting date, the acquiring authority no longer considers the conditions allowing it to take early possession of land are available, the authority will amend the general vesting declaration so that the period for the vesting of the land will be not less than three months from the date service of notice under section 6 was completed (section 6(1A) of the Compulsory Purchase (Vesting Declarations) Act 1981).

Stage 6: Compensation

95. What is the basis of compensation?

95.1 The rights to compensation for those affected by compulsory purchase – and the procedures for assessing the correct amount – are governed by a combination of legislation, case law and established practice. These are sometimes referred to collectively as the ‘compensation code’. However, there is no single, published document called the compensation code.

95.2 The overriding general principle of compulsory purchase compensation under the compensation code is the ‘equivalence principle’. This is the principle that a person who has an interest in land acquired compulsorily should be paid neither less nor more than the value of their loss other than where:

(a) a compulsory purchase order is confirmed with a direction for minimum compensation included where an owner of a listed building has deliberately allowed the building to fall into disrepair to justify its demolition and the development of the site (see What if the owner has deliberately allowed the listed building to fall into disrepair to justify its demolition?)

(b) a compulsory purchase order is confirmed with a direction applying section 14A of the Land Compensation Act 1961 included (see Section 27: Compulsory purchase orders which include directions to remove the prospects of planning permission from the assessment of compensation)

96. What are the elements of compensation where land is taken?

96.1 The compensation payable where land is taken is a single global figure, and in practice, the assessment of that compensation will involve various elements.

96.2 Broadly, the elements of compensation where land is taken are:

[the market value of the interest in the land taken]{#para98)

‘disturbance’ payments for losses caused by reason of losing possession of the land and other losses not directly based on the value of land, for example, costs arising from the relocation to a replacement property

loss payments for the distress and inconvenience of being required to sell and/or relocate from your property at a time not of your choosing

‘severance/injurious affection’ payments for the loss of value caused to retained land by reason of it being severed from the land taken, or caused as a result of the use to which the land is put

97. What are the elements of compensation where no land is taken?

97.1 Broadly, the elements of compensation where no land is taken are:

injurious affection

Part 1 Land Compensation Act 1973 claims

98. What is the market value of the interest in the land taken?

98.1 The value of land taken is the amount which it might be expected to realise if sold on the open market by a willing seller (Land Compensation Act 1961, section 5, rule 2), disregarding any effect on value of the scheme of the acquiring authority (known as the ‘no scheme’ principle). In addition to existing planning permissions, section 14 of the Land Compensation Act 1961 (as amended by section 189 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023) provides for certain assumptions as to what planning permissions might be granted in the no scheme world to be taken into account in determining the open market value of land (‘planning assumptions’).

98.2 Certificates of Appropriate Alternative Development may be used to indicate the planning permissions that could have been obtained in the no scheme world, which will affect any development value of the land (see Section 23 for guidance on Certificates of Appropriate Alternative Development). Alternatively, where the property is used for a purpose for which there is no general demand or market (e.g. a church) and the owner intends to reinstate elsewhere, the owner may be awarded compensation on the basis of the reasonable cost of equivalent reinstatement (see Land Compensation Act 1961, section 5, rule 5).

99. What are the planning assumptions?

99.1 Section 14 of the Land Compensation Act 1961[footnote 29] provides the legal framework for assessing compensation for the compulsory purchase of land in accordance with rule (2) of section 5 of the Land Compensation Act 1961 (determining open market value). The planning assumptions under section 14 (as amended) are as follows:

(i) subsection (2): account may be taken of

(a) any planning permission in force for development on the relevant land or other land at the relevant valuation date; and (b) the prospect of planning permission being granted on or after the relevant valuation date for development on the relevant land or other land other than for development for which planning permission is already in force at the relevant valuation date.

The prospects of planning permission under subsection (2)(b) are to be assessed on the assumptions set out in subsection (5) (see below) and otherwise in the circumstances known to the market at the relevant valuation date (subsection (2B)(b)).

(ii) subsection (2A): if a description of development is certified under section 17 of the 1961 Act as appropriate alternative development in relation to the relevant land or any part of it, it is to be taken as certain for the purposes of assessing the prospect of planning permission under subsection (2)(b) that:

(a) planning permission for that description of development would be, or would have been, granted on the relevant valuation date, and

(b) the permission would be, or would have been, granted subject to any conditions or pre-conditions given under section 17(5B) of the Land Compensation Act 1961

(iii) subsection (5): contains the basic assumptions referred to above under subsection 2(b) that:

(a) the scheme underlying the acquisition had been cancelled on the launch date;

(b) no action has been taken by the acquiring authority for the purposes of the scheme;

(c) there is no prospect of the same or a similar scheme being taken forward by the exercise of a statutory power or by compulsory purchase; and

(d) if the scheme is for a highway, no other highway would be constructed to meet the same need as the scheme.

(iv) subsection (6): defines the ‘launch date’ as:

(a) for a compulsory purchase order, the publication date of the notice required under section 11 of, or paragraph 2 of Schedule 1 to, the Acquisition of Land Act 1981;

(b) for any other order (such as under the Transport and Works Act 1992 or a development consent order under the Planning Act 2008) the date of first publication or service of the relevant notice; or

(c) for a special enactment, the date of first publication of the first notice required in connection with the acquisition.

100. On what date are the planning assumptions assessed?

100.1 The planning assumptions are assessed on the relevant valuation date (as defined in section 5A of the Land Compensation Act 1961) rather than the launch date of the scheme (even though the scheme is still assumed to have been cancelled on the launch date). This will avoid the need to reconstruct the planning regime that existed on the launch date, including old development plans, national planning policy and guidance. Also, that the planning assumptions are based on ‘the circumstances known to the market at the relevant valuation date’, which would include the provisions of the development plan. This removes the need for the specific references to the development plan which were contained in the previous section 16 of the Land Compensation Act 1961 that had become out of date and was subsequently repealed.

101. How should the value of the land be assessed in light of the ‘no scheme principle’?

101.1 Sections 6A to 6E of the Land Compensation Act 1961 (as amended)[footnote 30], set out how the value of the land should be assessed applying the ‘no scheme principle’.

101.2 Section 6A out the ‘no scheme principle’ that any increases or decreases in value caused by the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order, or the prospect of that scheme, must be disregarded. When applying the ‘no scheme principle’, the following 5 rules (i.e. the ‘no scheme rules’) are to be followed:

rule 1: it is to be assumed that the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order was cancelled on the relevant valuation date

rule 2: it is to be assumed that no action has been taken (including acquisition of any land, and any development or works) by the acquiring authority, or on behalf of the acquiring authority, wholly or mainly for the purposes of the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order. For example, where an acquiring authority has entered into an agreement with a developer to deliver a scheme underpinned by use of compulsory purchase powers, actions taken by the developer are actions taken by the acquiring authority for the purposes of this Rule. Any such action taken, including, for example, works carried out by that developer, should be assumed not to have been taken

rule 3: it is to be assumed that there is no prospect of the same scheme which is underlying the compulsory purchase order, or any other project to meet the same or substantially the same need as that being delivered by the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order, being carried out in the exercise of a statutory function or by the exercise of compulsory purchase powers

rule 4: it is to be assumed that no other projects would have been carried out in the exercise of a statutory function or by the exercise of compulsory purchase powers if the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order had been cancelled on the relevant valuation date

rule 5: if there was a reduction in the value of land as a result of—

(a) the prospect of the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order (including before the scheme or the compulsory acquisition in question was authorised)

(b) the fact that the land was blighted land as a result of the scheme underlying the compulsory purchase order

that reduction is to be disregarded. “Blighted land” in this regard means land of a description listed in Schedule 13 to the Town and Country Planning Act 1990

101.3 Section 6B provides that any increases in the value of the claimant’s other land, which is contiguous or adjacent to the land taken, is deducted from the compensation payable. This is known as ‘betterment’.

101.4 Section 6C provides that where a claimant is compensated for injurious affection for other land when land is taken for a scheme, and then that other land is subsequently subject to compulsory purchase for the purposes of the scheme, the compensation for the acquisition of the other land is to be reduced by the amount received for injurious affection.

101.5 Section 6D defines the ‘scheme’ for the purposes of establishing the no-scheme world. The default case, set out in subsection (1), is that the ‘scheme’ to be disregarded is the scheme of development underlying the compulsory acquisition. Subsection (2) makes special provision for new towns, urban development corporations and mayoral development corporations. Where land is acquired in connection with these areas, the ‘scheme’ is the development of any land for the purposes for which the area is or was designated.

101.6 Section 6D(3) and (4) also makes special provision. It provides that where land is acquired for development (including redevelopment, regeneration and improvement as per section 6D(7)) which is facilitated or made possible by a ‘relevant transport project’[footnote 31], ‘the scheme’ includes the relevant transport project.

102. Why is special provision made for relevant transport projects?

102.1 New transport projects often raise land values in the vicinity of stations or hubs which can facilitate development such as regeneration, redevelopment and improvement schemes. Where land is acquired for a development scheme, which is facilitated or made possible by a relevant transport project, the effect of Section 6D(3) is that the scheme to be disregarded includes the relevant transport project – subject to the qualifying conditions and safeguards in section 6E (see below). The intention of this special provision is to ensure an acquiring authority should not pay for land it is acquiring at values that are inflated by its own or others’ public investment in the relevant transport project.

102.2 Where it applies, the land in question will be valued as if the transport project as well as the development scheme had been cancelled on the relevant valuation date (defined in section 5A). The qualifying conditions and safeguards in section 6E(2) are, in summary that:

the development (including regeneration, redevelopment or improvement) of land in the vicinity of land comprised in the relevant transport project was part of the published justification for that relevant transport project

the instrument authorising the compulsory purchase of the land acquired for development was made or prepared in draft on or after 22 September 2017

the development land must be in the vicinity of land comprised in the relevant transport project

the works comprised in the relevant transport project are first opened for use no earlier than 22 September 2022

the compulsory purchase of the land acquired for development must be authorised within 5 years of the works comprised in the relevant transport project first opening for use

102.3 However, ‘the scheme’ for the purposes of assessing compensation payable to a person in respect of the compulsory acquisition of the land for development will not be treated as if it included the relevant transport project if the owner acquired the land after plans for the relevant transport project were announced but before either:

(a) 8 September 2016 (the day after the Neighbourhood Planning Bill was printed), in a case where the land was acquired for regeneration or redevelopment and regeneration or redevelopment was part of the published justification for the relevant transport project)

(b) in any other case, 1 May 2024 (the first day after the period of three months beginning with 31 January 2024 i.e. the day on which section 188 of the Levelling-up and Regeneration Act 2023 came into force (see section 6E(3A)(b) of the Land Compensation Act 1961[footnote 32])

102.4 This specific safeguard (under section 6E(3)) is intended to provide protection in circumstances where land was purchased:

on the basis of a public announcement whose effect was to provide a reasonable degree of certainty about the delivery of a relevant transport project at a particular location

before the government introduced legislation that made special provision for relevant transport projects

102.5 Where the specific safeguard applies, the ‘scheme’ will not be treated as if it included the relevant transport project in assessing the compensation payable in respect of the compulsory acquisition of that land. In such circumstances, any increase or decrease in the value of the owner’s land caused by the relevant transport project does not have to be disregarded.

103. When is a relevant transport project announced for the purposes of the specific safeguard in section 6E(3)?

103.1 Whether and/or when such a project is ‘announced’ is a question of fact in each case to be determined by the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) in the event of disagreement. The evidence put before the Upper Tribunal (Lands Chamber) could include, among other things, the following matters:

the inclusion of the relevant transport project, at or near a particular location, in an approved or adopted development plan document

the inclusion of the relevant transport project in an application for a development consent order or in a compulsory purchase order

the inclusion of the relevant transport project in a proposal contained in an application for, or in a draft, Transport and Works Act Order for the purposes of the Transport and Works Act 1992

the inclusion of the relevant transport project in any Bill put before Parliament

a decision announced by a Minister of, or of approval for, a relevant transport project at a particular location

104. What if the definition of the ‘scheme’ is disputed?

104.1 Section 6D(5) provides that if there is disagreement between parties as to the definition of the ‘scheme’ to be disregarded that this can be determined by the Upper Tribunal as a question of fact subject as follows.
